title: Antigen-Antibody Reactions & Agglutination

references.label: AABB Technical Manual
references.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB)

summary: Agglutination is the visible clumping that occurs when an antibody cross-links particulate antigens (whole cells or antigen-coated particles), forming a lattice large enough to see with the naked eye or under low magnification.
explanation: An antibody has multiple antigen-binding sites, so when the target antigen is on the surface of a particle (e.g. a red blood cell, a latex bead coated with antigen), a single antibody can bind two or more particles simultaneously, and multiple antibodies can cross-link many particles into a visible clump — this is the basis of blood typing reactions, many rapid antigen tests, and agglutination-based serologic assays. If the antigen is soluble rather than particulate, the equivalent antibody-mediated reaction instead forms a visible precipitate rather than agglutination. Reaction strength (graded, e.g. 4+ down to negative in many manual systems) reflects the amount and avidity of antibody present relative to antigen, and is read within a defined time window because reactions can weaken or strengthen non-specifically if read too early or too late.

comparison.right: Visible as a precipitate/line, not clumping

commonMisconceptions: Assuming any visible clumping is a true positive — rouleaux formation (stacked red cells, unrelated to antibody binding) and specimen artifacts can mimic weak agglutination and must be distinguished, often by saline replacement or microscopic examination.
